state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a map of a city, and you want to move all the buildings three blocks to the right. Would you just shift the whole map up three blocks, or would you adjust each building's position individually? This same concept applies to translating the graph of \(y=f(x)\) to \(y=f(x-3)\). Can you see how this relates to your current question about the translation by a vector \(\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]\)?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I see what you mean - so if we're moving things to the right, that would be a horizontal shift, not a vertical one? So the vector should have something in the top number, not the bottom? But I'm still confused about why it's to the right when the equation says (x-3) and not (x+3)...

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're trying to find your way home on a map, and you need to move three blocks to the right to reach your destination. Would you mistakenly go left instead? Just like in this real-world scenario, the expression \(x-3\) indicates a rightward shift, not a leftward one.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that don't directly address why f(x-a) shifts right (the core misconception), and while the student recognizes it should be horizontal in Turn 2, the final analogy about going home doesn't explain the counterintuitive nature of the transformation, leaving the student still confused about the direction.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use real-world analogies (city map, finding home), these analogies don't actually illuminate the mathematical concept—they simply restate the conclusion without explaining why x-3 produces a rightward shift, failing to ground the counterintuitive transformation in a concrete experience that would build understanding.
